title: Red Flags to Watch For When Hiring an Architect in Westchester
excerpt: Finding the right architect for your Westchester home project matters. Here's what to watch out for before you sign anything.
content:
Hiring an architect is one of the biggest decisions you'll make for a home renovation or new construction project. The wrong choice can cost you time, money, and headaches. Whether you're planning a kitchen remodel in Scarsdale, a second-story addition in Mamaroneck, or custom new construction anywhere across Westchester County, you need someone you can actually trust.

The problem is that not all architects work the same way. Some are great designers but terrible at managing budgets. Others disappear once the plans are done. Before you shake hands with anyone, here are the biggest red flags to watch for.

They Won't Talk About Project Management

If an architect tells you their job is just to draw pretty pictures, keep looking. A good architect needs to manage the entire process from start to finish. That means coordinating with builders, city inspectors, and material suppliers. It means catching problems before they become expensive mistakes on the job site.

This is especially important in towns like White Plains, Rye, and Eastchester, where every municipality has its own building department and permit process. Your architect should know these local requirements inside and out. They should walk you through what to expect, not act surprised when the building inspector shows up with questions.

The best setup is working with someone who is both a licensed architect in Westchester NY and a licensed general contractor. That dual expertise means one person understands both the design side and the construction side. There's no confusion about whether something is buildable or how much work it actually involves.

They Don't Listen to What You Want

Some architects come in with their own vision and try to force it on you. They talk more than they listen. They act like your ideas are beneath them. That's a huge warning sign.

Your architect should ask real questions about how you live in your home. What doesn't work about your current layout? How do you use your kitchen? Do you need more natural light? What's your timeline? They should sketch out ideas, show you options, and be willing to revise based on your feedback.

Whether you're planning home additions in Westchester or a major kitchen renovation in Pelham or Bronxville, this is your home. Your architect works for you, not the other way around.

They Disappear After the Drawings Are Done

Here's what happens with some architects: they hand you a set of plans and say "good luck." Then they're impossible to reach when questions come up during construction. The contractor finds a problem. The building inspector wants a clarification. You can't get your architect to return a call.

Your architect should be available throughout the entire build. They should visit the site, answer questions, and help solve problems when things don't go exactly as planned. This matters whether you're working on a residential architect in Scarsdale doing a historic restoration or working on new construction in Tarrytown or Hastings-on-Hudson.

A design-build firm in Westchester makes this easier because one person is responsible for both the design and the construction. There's nowhere to hide if something goes wrong. That accountability matters.

They Can't Explain Local Codes and Permitting

This is non-negotiable. Your architect needs to know building codes, zoning regulations, and local permit requirements. Every town in Westchester has its own process. Dobbs Ferry, Harrison, Ossining, and New Rochelle all have different departments and different people running them.

If your architect can't confidently explain what permits you'll need or what the approval process looks like, they're not ready for your project. This knowledge should be automatic for anyone working as a general contractor in Westchester or an architect in this county.
